name: Omoplata from Omoplata Control
summary: Omoplata from Omoplata Control is the shoulder-lock finish executed from established omoplata control, where the attacker's leg threads across the opponent's back to drive the isolated shoulder into external rotation until the opponent taps.
description: Master the omoplata finish from omoplata control position. Complete guide covering shoulder lock mechanics, finishing sequences, and defensive counters.
target_area: Shoulder joint (rotator cuff, capsule, AC joint)
overview:
The omoplata finish from omoplata control represents the culmination of one of Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu's most versatile attack sequences. Unlike omoplata entries from open guard or closed guard where the practitioner must first establish control, this variant begins with the shoulder already isolated and the opponent's posture compromised. The attacker's leg is already threaded across the opponent's upper back with the shin applying downward pressure, and the hip connection to the trapped shoulder is already established. This means the finish is about precise pressure application and preventing last-ditch escape attempts rather than fighting to secure the initial configuration.

The biomechanics of the finish center on progressive external rotation of the shoulder joint combined with forward pressure that drives the opponent's face toward the mat. The attacker sits perpendicular to the opponent's spine, using their hips as the fulcrum while the leg across the back acts as the lever arm. The critical detail that separates successful finishes from failed attempts is controlling the opponent's hip line to prevent the forward roll escape, which is the single most common defensive reaction at this stage.

In competition, the omoplata from established control carries a significantly higher success rate than entries from open positions because the opponent's defensive window has already closed on several escape options. The primary remaining defenses are the forward roll, posturing up, and arm extraction, each of which can be countered with proper technique. Understanding the relationship between hip angle, shoulder rotation, and base management transforms this position from a stalling point into a reliable finishing sequence.

injury_risks.recovery_time: 6-12 weeks for minor tears, 3-6 months for major tears

safety_considerations.application_speed: SLOW and progressive - 4-6 seconds minimum pressure increase
tap_signals: Physical hand tap on opponent or mat
Physical foot tap on opponent or mat
release_protocol: Immediately stop all forward pressure and rotation
Allow opponent to extract arm slowly
training_restrictions: Never spike or jerk the shoulder rotation
Never apply competition speed in training
Always allow opponent access to tap
Stop immediately if opponent rolls forward (escape attempt)
Never apply full finishing pressure until advanced belt level
Always control the rate of shoulder rotation

attacker.name: from Omoplata Control Attacker
attacker.description: Complete guide to finishing the omoplata from established control. Step-by-step shoulder lock mechanics, counter responses, and competition finishing strategies.
attacker.overview: Attacking the omoplata from established omoplata control is fundamentally different from chasing the finish during an entry. The control phase has already neutralized the opponent's most dangerous escape options, leaving a narrower set of defensive reactions to manage. Your leg is already across their upper back, their arm is isolated, and their posture is broken. The finish demands precise hip angle management, progressive shoulder rotation, and vigilant control of the opponent's hip line to prevent the forward roll. The attacker who understands that the omoplata finish is about incremental pressure rather than explosive force will find this position yields taps consistently in both training and competition.
key_principles: Maintain hip proximity to the trapped shoulder to prevent arm extraction and maximize rotational leverage
Control the opponent's far hip or belt line to shut down forward roll escape before applying finishing pressure
Apply shoulder rotation progressively by sitting up and leaning away, using body weight rather than muscular force
Keep the shin tight across the upper back with active downward knee pressure to prevent posturing
Monitor the opponent's free arm positioning as it telegraphs their next defensive reaction
Transition immediately to sweep or back take when the opponent commits weight to escape rather than forcing a compromised finish
Use the free leg as a dynamic base and secondary control point, posting or hooking the far hip as needed
setup_requirements: Omoplata control position established with leg threaded over opponent's shoulder and shin crossing upper back
Opponent's trapped arm isolated with shoulder in external rotation and limited defensive mobility
Hip connection tight to opponent's shoulder with proper perpendicular angle to their spine
Control grip established on opponent's belt, hip, or waistline to prevent forward roll escape
Free leg posted or hooking opponent's far hip to provide base and secondary control

execution_steps.description: From established omoplata control, grab the opponent's belt or far hip with your near hand. In no-gi, use a figure-four grip around their waist or hook their far hip crease. This grip is the foundation that prevents the forward roll escape and must be established before applying finishing pressure.

Walk your hips to achieve a perpendicular angle relative to the opponent's spine. Your hip bone should be nearly touching their trapped shoulder blade. This angle maximizes the rotational leverage on the shoulder joint and prevents the opponent from relieving pressure by turning into you.

Drive your knee toward the mat while keeping your shin tight across the opponent's upper back. This downward pressure flattens them and prevents any posturing attempt. The shin acts as a crossbar that pins their torso to the mat and isolates the shoulder for the finishing rotation.

Begin sitting up tall while maintaining your leg position and hip connection. Your torso should rise perpendicular to the opponent's body. As you sit up, your body weight shifts onto the fulcrum point at their shoulder, dramatically increasing the rotational pressure on the joint without requiring muscular effort.

Lean your upper body slightly away from the opponent while keeping your hips anchored near their shoulder. This creates a pulling force on their trapped arm through your leg position, increasing external rotation of the shoulder. The combination of sitting up and leaning away generates the primary finishing pressure through body mechanics.

execution_steps.action: Drive hips forward for final pressure
execution_steps.description: Drive your hips forward toward the opponent's head while maintaining the lean-away angle. This final forward pressure pushes their face toward the mat while simultaneously pulling their shoulder into maximum external rotation. Apply this pressure slowly and progressively over 4-6 seconds, giving the opponent time to recognize the submission and tap safely.

common_counters.counter: Forward roll escape where opponent tucks chin and rolls through the omoplata to escape shoulder pressure
common_counters.your_response: Maintain belt or hip grip to control roll speed. Follow the roll and transition to back control by inserting hooks as they complete the rotation. Alternatively, use the grip to completely block the roll before it initiates by anchoring their hips to the mat.

common_counters.counter: Posturing up by straightening the back and driving weight backward to relieve shoulder rotation pressure
common_counters.your_response: Increase shin pressure across upper back immediately and pull them back down with belt grip. If they achieve partial posture, transition to the omoplata sweep by driving forward with their upward momentum. Their elevated posture actually makes the sweep easier to execute.

common_counters.counter: Arm extraction where opponent rotates their elbow inward and pulls the trapped arm free from the leg configuration
common_counters.your_response: If extraction begins, increase knee pressure toward the mat to tighten the leg clamp on their arm. If the arm continues extracting, immediately transition to triangle choke since their head is already positioned between your legs, or switch to armbar by controlling their wrist and swinging your leg over their face.

common_counters.counter: Stacking defense where opponent drives forward and presses their weight into the attacker to relieve rotation and compress the guard
common_counters.your_response: Move hips laterally away from the opponent to redirect their forward pressure into shoulder rotation. Their stacking attempt actually increases the submission pressure when you angle away properly. Use your free leg to hook their far hip and pull yourself into a sharper finishing angle.

common_errors.error: Allowing space between hips and opponent's trapped shoulder before applying finishing pressure
common_errors.consequence: Opponent can sit up, relieve shoulder rotation, and initiate escape sequences including arm extraction and forward roll
common_errors.correction: Keep your hip bone nearly touching their shoulder blade throughout the finish. Walk your hips closer before initiating any finishing pressure and maintain that proximity as you sit up and lean away.

common_errors.error: Attempting to finish with muscular force rather than progressive body mechanics
common_errors.consequence: Rapid fatigue, loss of positional control, and opponent gains time to execute defensive reactions while you tire
common_errors.correction: Use sitting up tall and leaning away to generate rotational pressure through body weight and leverage. The finish should feel effortless when the angle and positioning are correct.

common_errors.error: Neglecting belt or hip grip before applying finishing pressure
common_errors.consequence: Opponent executes the forward roll escape, the single highest percentage defense against the omoplata finish
common_errors.correction: Always establish and maintain a grip on the opponent's belt, hip, or waistline before beginning the finishing sequence. This grip is non-negotiable for a reliable finish.

common_errors.error: Applying finishing pressure too quickly or explosively in training
common_errors.consequence: Risk of serious shoulder injury to training partner including rotator cuff tears and labrum damage
common_errors.correction: Apply finishing pressure over a minimum of 4-6 seconds. The shoulder joint is vulnerable to sudden rotational force and injuries can be severe and career-ending.

common_errors.error: Failing to control the opponent's free arm during the finishing sequence
common_errors.consequence: Opponent uses free arm to post on the mat, create base, and generate enough leverage to posture up or turn into the attacker
common_errors.correction: Monitor the free arm constantly. Use your free hand to control their wrist or elbow, or position your body so their posting hand is ineffective.

common_errors.error: Insisting on the finish when the opponent has partially escaped rather than transitioning to alternative attacks
common_errors.consequence: Loss of the entire position as the opponent completes their escape while you chase a submission that is no longer available
common_errors.correction: Recognize when the omoplata control has been compromised and transition immediately to sweep, back take, triangle, or armbar rather than forcing a low-percentage finish.

training_progressions.description: Partner holds still in omoplata control bottom position. Practice the full finishing sequence focusing on hip angle, sitting up tall, leaning away, and progressive forward pressure. No resistance. 20 repetitions per side. Focus entirely on feeling correct body mechanics.

training_progressions.focus: Identifying and responding to defensive reactions
training_progressions.description: Partner performs one specific escape attempt at 50% speed. Practice the correct counter for each of the four main defenses: forward roll, posture up, arm extraction, and stacking. 10 repetitions per defense per side. Build pattern recognition before combining defenses.

training_progressions.focus: Completing the finish against progressive resistance
training_progressions.description: Partner defends with 75% intensity using any combination of escapes. Practice maintaining control, applying finishing pressure, and transitioning to alternative attacks when the finish is defended. 5-minute rounds with reset after each finish or escape.

training_progressions.focus: Finishing under time pressure and full resistance
training_progressions.description: Full-resistance positional sparring starting from omoplata control. Attacker must finish or transition to a dominant position within 60 seconds. Defender uses full defensive arsenal. Track finish rate and analyze which defensive reactions cause the most difficulty.

flashcards.question: What anatomical structures does the omoplata primarily attack and what creates the tapping pressure?
flashcards.answer: The omoplata primarily attacks the shoulder joint through forced external rotation. The rotational pressure targets the rotator cuff muscles and tendons, the shoulder capsule, the AC joint, and in extreme cases the labrum. The tapping pressure comes from the combination of the attacker's leg acting as a lever across the upper back while the hips serve as the fulcrum, progressively rotating the shoulder beyond its natural range of motion.

flashcards.question: Your opponent begins tucking their chin and loading weight forward for a roll escape - what immediate adjustment prevents this?
flashcards.answer: Immediately tighten your grip on their belt or far hip to anchor their hips to the mat and block the forward momentum needed for the roll. Simultaneously increase your shin pressure across their upper back to flatten them. If the roll has already initiated, do not fight it but instead follow through and transition to back control by maintaining your leg position and inserting hooks as they complete the rotation. The belt grip controls whether the roll happens at all.

flashcards.question: What are the key indicators that the shoulder joint has reached its breaking point and a tap is imminent?
flashcards.answer: Indicators include the opponent suddenly tensing their entire body and stopping all escape attempts, audible distress sounds or sharp inhalation, the trapped arm going limp or the hand opening from a fist, the opponent's free hand moving toward you or the mat to tap rather than continuing defensive posting, and visible elevation of the shoulder blade away from the ribcage indicating the joint is at maximum rotation. Any of these signals should prompt you to hold current pressure without increasing it.

flashcards.question: What is the correct hip angle relative to the opponent's spine for maximum finishing pressure?
flashcards.answer: Your hips should be positioned perpendicular to the opponent's spine, with your hip bone nearly touching their trapped shoulder blade. This angle creates the optimal fulcrum point for shoulder rotation. If your hips drift too far toward their head or feet, the rotational leverage decreases significantly. As you apply the finish by sitting up and leaning away, maintain this perpendicular relationship while driving your hips forward to create the final rotation that generates the tap.

flashcards.question: How should you release the omoplata immediately after your training partner taps?
flashcards.answer: Immediately stop all forward pressure and shoulder rotation upon feeling or hearing the tap. Release the downward pressure of your shin across their back by lifting your knee. Unwind your hip position to neutral, moving away from their trapped shoulder. Allow your partner to slowly extract their arm at their own pace without pulling it free for them, as forced extraction can cause additional injury. Check that your partner has full range of motion and no pain before resuming training.

flashcards.question: Your opponent partially postures up and you feel your shin sliding off their back - what grip adjustment prevents losing the position?
flashcards.answer: Immediately pull with your belt or hip grip to bring them back down while simultaneously driving your knee back toward the mat to reseat the shin across their upper back. If the shin has slipped too far, use your free hand to grab their wrist on the trapped arm side to prevent arm extraction while you reposition. If they achieve significant posture, abandon the finish and transition to the omoplata sweep by driving forward into their elevated center of gravity, which is actually easier to sweep when they are upright.

flashcards.question: What is the most common finishing error that leads to training partner injuries with the omoplata?
flashcards.answer: The most dangerous error is applying finishing pressure too quickly or with a sudden jerking motion. The shoulder joint is highly susceptible to rotational force injuries, and the omoplata generates enormous mechanical advantage through the lever system of the legs. A sudden application of force can tear the rotator cuff or damage the labrum before the opponent has time to recognize the submission and tap. Finishing pressure must always be applied progressively over a minimum of 4-6 seconds, giving the opponent adequate time to tap safely.

flashcards.question: Your opponent extracts their trapped arm halfway out of the omoplata - what is the highest percentage follow-up attack?
flashcards.answer: The highest percentage follow-up when the arm is partially extracted is the triangle choke. Their head is already positioned between your legs from the omoplata configuration, and as they pull the arm free, they create the asymmetric arm position needed for the triangle. Throw your leg that was across their back over the back of their neck and lock the triangle figure-four. The transition is fast because you are already in the correct body position and only need to reconfigure your legs rather than create an entirely new attacking angle.

flashcards.question: In competition with 30 seconds remaining, how do you accelerate the omoplata finish while maintaining safety?
flashcards.answer: Accelerate the finish by perfecting your control rather than increasing force speed. Immediately secure the deepest possible belt grip and flatten the opponent with maximum shin pressure. Sit up explosively to a tall perpendicular position and lean away to load the shoulder quickly. Drive hips forward with steady progressive pressure. The acceleration comes from eliminating the setup time between control and finish, not from applying force faster. You can compress a 15-second finishing sequence into 6-8 seconds by being more decisive in your positioning while still maintaining safe progressive pressure on the joint.

flashcards.question: What distinguishes the omoplata finish from omoplata control versus finishing during the initial entry?
flashcards.answer: From established control, the opponent's defensive window has narrowed considerably. The forward roll, posturing, and arm extraction are their only remaining options, whereas during entry they could have defended the leg threading, blocked the hip switch, or maintained posture before control was established. The control position means you already have the belt grip, perpendicular hip angle, and shin across the back established. The finish is purely about progressive pressure application and counter defense rather than simultaneously securing control and attacking. This is why the finish rate from established control is significantly higher than from entry positions.

defender.name: from Omoplata Control Defender
defender.description: Essential defensive guide against the omoplata finish from control position. Recognition cues, escape timing, and safe defensive strategies explained.
defender.overview: Defending the omoplata from established omoplata control is one of the more urgent defensive situations in BJJ because the attacker already has the mechanical advantage of a secured position. Your shoulder is already isolated, their leg is across your back, and their hips are close to your trapped shoulder. The defensive window is narrowing and every second spent without a purposeful escape attempt brings you closer to the tap. The defender must recognize which phase of the finish the attacker is in and select the appropriate defensive response. The three primary escapes each target a different stage of the finishing sequence, and attempting the wrong escape at the wrong time can accelerate the submission rather than prevent it. Understanding the mechanics from both sides is essential for mounting an effective defense.
key_principles: Posture immediately and continuously to relieve rotational pressure on the shoulder before the attacker can secure finishing angle
Protect the trapped arm by turning the elbow inward and keeping it tight to your body to resist external rotation
Control the attacker's hips with your free hand to prevent them from achieving perpendicular finishing angle
Commit fully to one escape path rather than attempting half-measures that waste energy and surrender position
Recognize the transition between control phase and finishing phase to time your escape during the gap between the two
Keep your base wide with your free arm to prevent being flattened, which eliminates most escape options
recognition_cues: Attacker's shin is tight across your upper back with their knee driving downward, creating a bar of pressure across your shoulder blades
Your arm is trapped between their legs with limited ability to pull it free, and you feel increasing external rotation pressure on your shoulder
Attacker is gripping your belt, hip, or waistline with their near hand, which signals they are preparing to apply finishing pressure
Attacker begins sitting up tall and leaning away from you, which is the primary finishing mechanic that generates shoulder rotation
You feel your face being driven toward the mat as the attacker drives their hips forward in the final phase of the finish

defensive_options.action: Forward roll escape by tucking chin and rolling through the omoplata to relieve shoulder pressure and escape to top position
defensive_options.when_to_use: Early in the finishing sequence before the attacker has secured a deep belt grip. Must be attempted before they anchor your hips to the mat.
defensive_options.if_successful: You escape the shoulder lock and end up in a scramble or recover to a neutral position with the attacker still attempting to re-establish control
defensive_options.risk: If the attacker follows the roll and maintains leg position, they can transition to back control. A failed roll can also worsen your position by flattening you completely.

defensive_options.action: Posture up aggressively by straightening your back, driving your weight backward, and using your free arm to create a strong posting base
defensive_options.when_to_use: When the attacker has not yet increased their shin pressure across your back and you still have enough space to extend your spine upward
defensive_options.if_successful: You relieve shoulder rotation pressure and create space to begin extracting your trapped arm or transition to a defensive guard recovery
defensive_options.risk: The attacker may use your upward momentum against you by transitioning to the omoplata sweep, driving you over and landing in mount or side control.

defensive_options.action: Arm extraction by rotating your elbow inward and pulling the trapped arm free while using your free hand to push against the attacker's controlling leg
defensive_options.when_to_use: When you have managed to create even slight space between the attacker's leg and your shoulder through posturing or lateral movement
defensive_options.if_successful: You free your arm from the omoplata configuration and can recover to guard, though the attacker may immediately transition to triangle or armbar
defensive_options.risk: Partial extraction can leave you in a worse position if the attacker transitions to triangle choke as your arm comes free, since your head is already between their legs.

escape_paths: Forward roll through the omoplata before belt grip is secured, continuing the roll to end up in a top scramble position
Posture and arm extraction combination where you create space with posture then work the elbow inward to slip the arm free
Lateral hip movement away from the attacker to reduce shoulder rotation angle, buying time to work posture or roll escape

favorable_outcomes.how: Execute the forward roll escape before the attacker can anchor your hips with their belt grip, or posture up enough to neutralize the finishing pressure and force the attacker to reset their control

Successfully extract the trapped arm through elbow rotation and pulling while creating space with posture, then immediately close your guard to prevent the attacker from transitioning to triangle or armbar

common_errors.error: Waiting too long to initiate escape, allowing the attacker to fully secure belt grip and finishing angle
common_errors.consequence: All escape options become significantly harder once the attacker has perpendicular hip angle, deep belt grip, and shin locked across the back. The submission becomes nearly inescapable at this stage.
common_errors.correction: Begin your primary escape attempt immediately when you recognize the attacker is transitioning from control to finishing. The gap between these phases is your best escape window.

common_errors.error: Attempting a half-hearted forward roll without committing fully to the movement
common_errors.consequence: You end up flattened on the mat with your shoulder exposed and the attacker still in full control, having wasted energy without improving your position
common_errors.correction: Commit completely to the roll by tucking your chin, loading your weight onto your free posting hand, and driving through the roll with explosive hip extension. A committed roll either works or gives you a scramble.

common_errors.error: Pulling the trapped arm straight back rather than rotating the elbow inward during extraction attempts
common_errors.consequence: Straight pulling fights against the mechanical advantage of the attacker's leg position and wastes energy without creating meaningful progress toward extraction
common_errors.correction: Rotate your elbow inward toward your own centerline first, then pull the arm out along the path of least resistance. The rotation changes the angle of the arm relative to the attacker's leg clamp and creates the space needed for extraction.

common_errors.error: Neglecting to tap when the shoulder reaches maximum rotation, attempting to tough through the submission
common_errors.consequence: Serious shoulder injury including rotator cuff tears, labrum damage, or AC joint separation that can require surgery and months of recovery
common_errors.correction: Tap immediately when you feel the shoulder reaching its rotational limit. The omoplata generates enormous mechanical advantage and the difference between a tap and an injury is measured in fractions of a second. No training roll is worth a shoulder reconstruction.

flashcards.question: What are the earliest recognition cues that the omoplata finish is being initiated from control position?
flashcards.answer: The earliest cues are the attacker securing a grip on your belt or far hip, and beginning to adjust their hip angle to perpendicular. You will feel increased pressure from their shin across your upper back as they drive their knee down, and their body will begin rising as they sit up tall. Recognizing these setup movements gives you the best chance to initiate escape before the finishing pressure becomes overwhelming.

flashcards.question: When should you tap to the omoplata to prevent injury, and what signals indicate you are approaching the danger threshold?
flashcards.answer: Tap when you feel sharp pain in the shoulder joint, when you sense the shoulder reaching the end of its natural range of external rotation, or when the pressure transitions from uncomfortable to painful. Warning signals include a stretching sensation deep in the shoulder capsule, inability to resist the rotation with muscular effort, and the feeling that the shoulder is about to pop or shift. Tap early and tap clearly. Shoulder injuries from omoplatas are among the most serious in BJJ and often require surgical intervention.

flashcards.question: What is the optimal timing window for the forward roll escape against the omoplata finish?
flashcards.answer: The optimal window is after the attacker has committed to the finishing sequence by sitting up but before they have secured a deep belt or hip grip. Once the belt grip is locked in, the roll becomes extremely difficult because they can anchor your hips to the mat. If you feel them reaching for your belt, that is your trigger to initiate the roll immediately. A well-timed roll when the attacker is sitting up can use their own elevated position against them.

flashcards.question: What defensive options remain when both the forward roll and posturing escapes have failed?
flashcards.answer: When the primary escapes have failed, your remaining options are arm extraction through elbow rotation and lateral hip movement to reduce the finishing angle. Focus on turning your elbow inward while pushing against their controlling leg with your free hand. If extraction fails, move your hips laterally away from the attacker to reduce the shoulder rotation angle and buy time. If all escape options are exhausted and you feel increasing shoulder pressure, tap immediately rather than risk injury by attempting to endure the submission.

training_progressions.focus: Learning each escape technique individually without resistance
training_progressions.description: Practice the forward roll, posture escape, and arm extraction individually with a cooperative partner. 15 repetitions of each escape per side. Focus on correct body mechanics and understanding the movement pattern before adding any resistance.

training_progressions.focus: Identifying the correct escape for each phase of the finishing sequence
training_progressions.description: Partner slowly transitions through the finishing sequence while defender practices recognizing which phase they are in and selecting the appropriate escape. 50% speed with verbal cues initially, progressing to reading body position only.

Partner applies the omoplata finish at 50-75% intensity while defender attempts escapes. Track success rate for each escape type. 5-minute rounds with reset after each successful escape or submission. Identify which defensive reactions need the most work.

Full-resistance positional sparring starting from omoplata control. Defender must escape or survive for 60 seconds. Track escape rate and common failure points. Debrief after each round to analyze what defensive option was appropriate at each moment.
